notes.title: Start here: a Next.js app, a Prisma schema and a background worker
notes.body:
Linkwarden is a self-hosted bookmark manager. A Next.js app (`linkwarden/apps/web`) handles users, collections and links; a separate worker (`linkwarden/apps/worker`) preserves each link in the background as a screenshot, PDF, readable text and more, and pushes it into Meilisearch for search. Both talk to one Postgres database through Prisma.

Read these from `linkwarden/fabledocs/upskill/`, in order:

1. `00-fast-track.md`: how to run it, the first ten files, and two flows (adding a link, preserving it).
2. `03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md`: every side effect the system has, and how each one is made safe to repeat.
3. `03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md`: validation layers, the authentication chain and the authorization rules.

The fast track's ten files are the right ones to keep open, above all `apps/worker/worker.ts` and `apps/worker/lib/archiveHandler.ts`. The guides mark some claims *investigate*; treat every claim as something to confirm in the code, including the ones that are not marked.

excerpts.quote: Goal: by Sunday night you can run Linkwarden locally, trace two end-to-end flows aloud

notes.title: Concept: making background work safe to repeat
notes.body:
A background worker keeps picking up work, and any piece of work can half-happen: the process crashes, a page hangs, a remote service times out. Reliability means deciding, for each effect, what happens next time. Learn these terms from the side-effects guide before you read the code:

- **Idempotency marker**: a column that records an effect is done, checked before acting.
- **At-least-once / at-most-once**: whether an effect may repeat, or may be skipped, after a failure.
- **Compensation**: undoing a partial effect when the situation changed underneath it.
- **Bulkhead** and **supervision**: keeping one failure from spreading, and restarting what died.

Then, for each loop in `apps/worker/workers/`, find three things: the `where` clause that selects its batch, the column it writes afterwards, and whether that write sits after the effect or in a `finally`. In `archiveHandler.ts`, read the `finally` block line by line, including its `else` branch. In `linkIndexing.ts`, check what happens when each awaited call fails. Finally, read `apps/worker/index.ts` and `linkProcessing.ts` for what restarts what.

excerpts.quote: A **side effect** is anything a request/job does beyond returning a value: writes, emails, external calls.

readMore.why: The archiving engine and its finally block.

notes.title: Concept: authentication, then authorization per controller
notes.body:
Authentication answers "who is calling"; authorization answers "may they do this to this collection". Linkwarden does the first in one chain and the second separately inside each controller, using a helper that returns data rather than a yes/no.

Read the validation-and-auth guide, then confirm each step in code:

- `apps/web/lib/api/verifyToken.ts`: list each check in order and what the function returns when one fails.
- `apps/web/lib/api/getPermission.ts`: compare the two branches (by link id, by collection id) and note which inputs each query actually uses.
- `apps/web/lib/api/controllers/links/linkId/updateLinkById.ts`: write down every early `return` with its status code and condition, and find where files on disk are touched relative to the database update.
- `apps/web/pages/api/v1/links/index.ts`: look at how query-string values are converted before they reach `getLinks`.

As you go, note which HTTP status codes the repo uses for which kind of refusal.

excerpts.quote: The security spine in one page.

notes.title: lastPreserved is the pipeline key
notes.body:
`getLinkBatchFairly` in `links` mode selects links with `url: { not: null }` and `lastPreserved: null`. `archiveHandler` sets `lastPreserved` in its `finally` block whether archiving succeeded or not, so a link leaves the queue after one pass. The fast track calls this the idempotency key of the whole pipeline.

- *A per-link Redis lock*: the worker uses no Redis or locks; it relies on being a single worker.
- *A unique index on Link.url*: there is none, and an index would not stop repeated archiving of one row.
- *A flag the web app sets*: the web app does not mark links preserved; the worker does.

readMore.why: Flow B and the pause-and-predict question.

notes.title: A failed archive still counts as done
notes.body:
The work runs inside `try { await Promise.race(...) } catch { ...; throw err } finally { ... }`. The `finally` runs after the throw too: it re-reads the link and, if it exists, sets `lastPreserved` to now and every format still empty (`readable`, `image`, `monolith`, `pdf`, `preview`) to `"unavailable"`, plus `indexVersion: null`.

- *lastPreserved stays null*: `finally` always stamps it while the row exists, so the link is not retried.
- *The row is deleted*: rows are never deleted here; files are removed only when the row is already gone.
- *A retry counter with backoff*: the guide lists retry-with-backoff as not present.

readMore.why: The inventory row for preservation files.

notes.title: Why archiving is at most once
notes.body:
The guide's reasoning: indexing is at least once because a duplicate index write is harmless, while archiving is at most once because repeating the archive of a *poison* URL (one that always fails or hangs until the browser timeout) is not harmless; it would occupy the worker on every pass. So a failed link is stamped done with its missing formats marked `unavailable`.

- *Prisma cannot store a failure*: it does store one; `"unavailable"` in each format column is exactly that.
- *The Wayback copy covers it*: `sendToWayback` is optional, fire-and-forget, and says nothing about the local archive.
- *Indexing waits for lastPreserved*: the indexing loop selects on `indexVersion`, not on `lastPreserved`.

excerpts.quote: duplicate indexing is harmless, duplicate archiving of a poison URL is not

readMore.why: The indexing loop and its where clause.

notes.title: The indexing loop marks even on a wait error
notes.body:
After `addDocuments`, the loop calls `waitForTask(...)` with a `.catch` that only logs "Error indexing links". Execution then continues to `prisma.link.updateMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } }, data: { indexVersion: MEILI_INDEX_VERSION } })`. So a timed-out wait still marks the whole batch as indexed. The guide's row ("row stays stale-versioned until success") holds when `addDocuments` itself throws, but not for this error; the code is what runs.

- *Stays stale and is resent*: the update runs right after the caught error.
- *Set to null*: `null` is what `archiveHandler` writes to request re-indexing; this loop writes the current version.
- *The loop throws*: the `.catch` swallows the rejection, so nothing propagates.

readMore.why: The inventory row for Meilisearch writes.

notes.title: Compensation when the link vanishes
notes.body:
The `finally` block runs `prisma.link.findUnique({ where: { id: link.id } })`. If the user deleted the link meanwhile, `finalLink` is null and the `else` branch calls `removeFiles(link.id, link.collectionId)`, deleting the files this run had already written. The guide calls this compensation.

- *Recreates the row*: nothing in the worker creates link rows from an archive.
- *Throws and restarts the worker*: `removeFiles` runs normally; nothing here crashes the process.
- *A tombstone row*: there is no row left to update, which is why the code removes files instead.

notes.title: A tiny supervisor respawns the worker
notes.body:
`apps/worker/index.ts` is the entry point (`tsx index.ts` in the package scripts). It spawns `tsx worker.ts` as a child process and, on its `exit` event, logs the code and signal and calls `setTimeout(launch, 5000)`. A crash in any loop therefore brings all loops back after five seconds.

- *PM2*: the worker package runs plain `tsx`; no process manager is used.
- *The web app starts a worker*: the web `/api/v1/worker` route only returns stats for the admin.
- *Nothing restarts it*: the supervisor in `index.ts` does.

readMore.why: Supervision and rotation in the reliability toolkit.

notes.title: A browser lives at most 30 minutes
notes.body:
At the top of each `while (true)` pass, `linkProcessing` checks `Date.now() - browserStartTs >= BROWSER_MAX_AGE_MS`, where the constant is `30 * 60 * 1000`, and calls `restartBrowser("30-minute rotation")`. That keeps a long-running Chromium from clogging up.

- *After every batch of 5*: `ARCHIVE_TAKE_COUNT` sizes a batch; it does not trigger a restart.
- *Only on disconnect*: a disconnect also triggers a restart in the per-link `catch`, but the timed rotation runs regardless.
- *Once a day*: the age limit is thirty minutes, not a daily schedule.

notes.title: Only owners move links
notes.body:
`isCollectionOwner` is true only when the caller owns both the current and the target collection. For a member it is false, and since the target id differs from `collectionIsAccessible?.id`, `unauthorizedSwitchCollection` is true. The controller returns status 401 with "You can't move a link to/from a collection you don't own." The repo uses 401 for authorization refusals, which the guide flags as a contract quirk.

- *canUpdate covers it*: `canUpdate` allows edits within the collection; moving is checked first and refused.
- *403*: correct HTTP semantics, but not what this code returns.
- *canCreate in the target*: `canCreate` is never consulted for a move.

readMore.why: The authorization table row for moving links.

notes.title: getPermission returns data, not a verdict
notes.body:
With a `linkId`, `getPermission` runs `prisma.collection.findFirst({ where: { links: { some: { id: linkId } } }, include: { members: true } })`. `userId` is not in that query, so it returns the link's collection and its members for anyone. Each controller must then compare `ownerId` and `members` with the caller. The `collectionId` branch is different: it does filter on owner or member.

- *null*: that describes the `collectionId` branch, not the `linkId` one.
- *A 401 response object*: the helper returns a Prisma result, never a response.
- *An empty members list*: `include: { members: true }` returns them all.

readMore.why: The guide note on this sharp edge.

notes.title: Files go before the database write
notes.body:
When `data.url` is valid and differs from `oldLink.url`, the controller runs `await removeFiles(oldLink.id, oldLink.collectionId)` and only then reaches `prisma.link.update`. If that update then fails, the old preview and archives are already gone while the row still points at them. The guide lists this as a wrong-order destructive effect.

- *After commit, in a hook*: there is no post-commit hook; the call sits before the update.
- *When the worker re-archives*: the worker writes new files; this deletion happens in the web request.
- *Not at all*: `removeFiles` is called on any valid URL change.

readMore.why: Side effect in a risky place, flag 2.

notes.title: Revocation is a database lookup
notes.body:
`verifyToken` decodes the NextAuth JWT, checks there is a user id, checks `token.exp` by hand, then runs `prisma.accessToken.findFirst({ where: { token: token.jti, revoked: true } })`. A hit returns the string "Your session has expired, please log in again." and the caller refuses the request. That lookup is what makes a signed, unexpired token revocable.

- *The decoded token*: a valid signature and exp are not enough once the jti is revoked.
- *A 403 status object*: `verifyToken` returns either a JWT or a message string, never a status.
- *A fresh token*: nothing here issues tokens.

readMore.why: The authentication chain as the guide describes it.

notes.title: Query coercion with Number
notes.body:
The GET branch builds `convertedData` with `sort: Number(req.query.sort as string)`. `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, and nothing checks it, so `getLinks` receives `sort: NaN`. The validation map in the guide marks this manual coercion as weak, a known gap ("NaN passes").

- *0 as a default*: `Number` does not fall back to 0 for text such as abc; blank strings are what become 0.
- *undefined*: `sort` has no conditional like `cursor` has; it is always converted.
- *A 400*: the route has no validation for query values.

readMore.why: The validation map row for route coercion.
